theory.intro: Displacement, velocity and acceleration are joined by calculus. Differentiating takes you from $x$ to $v$ to $a$; integrating takes you back the other way, using sufficient independent given conditions to find the constants.
facts: Differentiating goes $x \to v \to a$, and integrating goes $a \to v \to x$.
Every integration introduces a constant. Sufficient independent conditions are needed to find the constants; these can include displacement values at two different times.
The **displacement** of a particle over $t = p$ to $t = q$ is $x(q) - x(p)$, and it may be negative.
The **distance travelled** is the total length of path covered, so it is never negative.
The particle changes direction at a time where $v = 0$ and $v$ changes sign there.
If the particle changes direction inside an interval, split the interval at that time and add the distance of each leg.
A particle is **speeding up** when $v$ and $a$ have the same sign, and slowing down when their signs differ.
A positive acceleration alone does not mean speeding up: a particle with $v < 0$ and $a > 0$ is slowing down.
steps: Identify which of $x$, $v$ or $a$ is given, then differentiate or integrate to reach the one you need.
Use the given conditions to form enough independent equations to find the constants produced by integration.
To find when the particle is at rest, set $v = 0$ and solve for $t \ge 0$. Before concluding that the particle changes direction at an interior zero, check that $v$ changes sign across that time.
For distance travelled, split the interval at each time of rest and add the size of each change in displacement.

workedExamples.question_text: A particle has acceleration $a(t)=8t-6$ m/s² and velocity $v(2)=9$ m/s. Find its velocity as a function of time.
A particle has acceleration $a(t)=12\cos(4t)$ m/s², where $t$ is in seconds and angles are in radians. Its initial velocity is $-1$ m/s. Find $v(t)$.
A particle has velocity $v(t)=6t^2-4t+3$ m/s. Its displacement is $8$ m when $t=1$ s. Find its displacement function.
A particle has acceleration $a(t)=8t-4$ m/s², with $v(0)=3$ m/s and $x(0)=-2$ m. Find its velocity and displacement functions.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}v(t)&=\int(8t-4)\,dt\\&=4t^2-4t+C\end{align*}$
Using $v(0)=3$ gives $C=3$, so $v(t)=4t^2-4t+3$ m/s.
$\begin{align*}x(t)&=\int(4t^2-4t+3)\,dt\\&=\frac43t^3-2t^2+3t+D\end{align*}$
Using $x(0)=-2$ gives $D=-2$, so $x(t)=\frac43t^3-2t^2+3t-2$ m.

workedExamples.question_text: A particle has acceleration $a(t)=18t-8$ m/s². Its displacement is $2$ m at $t=0$ and $10$ m at $t=2$ s. Find its displacement function.
A particle has displacement $x(t)=t^3+3t+2$ metres. Find its displacement from $t=1$ to $t=3$ seconds, first using the displacement function and then using a definite integral of velocity.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}x(1)&=1+3+2\\&=6\text{ m}\\x(3)&=27+9+2\\&=38\text{ m}\end{align*}$
The displacement is $x(3)-x(1)=38-6=32$ m.
Differentiating gives $v(t)=3t^2+3$ m/s. Equivalently:
$\begin{align*}\int_1^3v(t)\,dt&=\int_1^3(3t^2+3)\,dt\\&=[t^3+3t]_1^3\\&=36-4\\&=32\text{ m}\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text:
A particle has displacement $x(t)=t^3-12t^2+36t+1$ metres for $0\le t\le7$ seconds.
(a) Find its velocity and acceleration.
(b) Find when it changes direction.
(c) Find its displacement and distance travelled over the interval.
(d) Find the open intervals during which it is speeding up.
workedExamples.solution_text:
(a)
$\begin{align*}v(t)&=\frac{dx}{dt}\\&=3t^2-24t+36\\&=3(t-2)(t-6)\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}a(t)&=\frac{dv}{dt}\\&=6t-24\\&=6(t-4)\end{align*}$
Velocity is measured in m/s and acceleration in m/s².
(b) Setting $v(t)=0$ gives $t=2$ or $t=6$. Velocity is positive for $0\le t<2$, negative for $2<t<6$, and positive for $6<t\le7$. It changes sign at both zeros, so the particle changes direction at $2$ s and $6$ s.
(c) The displacements at the endpoints and turning times are $x(0)=1$, $x(2)=33$, $x(6)=1$ and $x(7)=8$ metres.
$\begin{align*}\text{Displacement}&=x(7)-x(0)\\&=8-1\\&=7\text{ m}\end{align*}$
$\begin{align*}\text{Distance}&=|33-1|+|1-33|+|8-1|\\&=32+32+7\\&=71\text{ m}\end{align*}$
(d) Acceleration is negative before $t=4$ and positive after $t=4$. Velocity and acceleration are both negative on $2<t<4$ and both positive on $6<t<7$. The particle is speeding up on these intervals. On $4<t<6$, positive acceleration accompanies negative velocity, so it is slowing down.

workedExamples.question_text: A particle has acceleration $a(t)=12t-30$ m/s², with $v(0)=18$ m/s and $x(0)=0$ m. Find the distance it travels in the first $5$ seconds.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}v(t)&=\int(12t-30)\,dt\\&=6t^2-30t+C\end{align*}$
Using $v(0)=18$ gives $C=18$.
$\begin{align*}x(t)&=\int(6t^2-30t+18)\,dt\\&=2t^3-15t^2+18t+D\end{align*}$
Using $x(0)=0$ gives $D=0$.
At rest:
$\begin{align*}6t^2-30t+18&=0\\t^2-5t+3&=0\\t&=\frac{5\pm\sqrt{13}}2\end{align*}$
Both times lie inside $0<t<5$. Write $r=\frac{5-\sqrt{13}}2$ and $s=\frac{5+\sqrt{13}}2$. Velocity is positive before $r$, negative between $r$ and $s$, and positive after $s$.
At either root, $t^2=5t-3$ and $t^3=22t-15$, so:
$\begin{align*}x(t)&=2(22t-15)-15(5t-3)+18t\\&=15-13t\end{align*}$
Thus $x(r)=\frac{-35+13\sqrt{13}}2$, $x(s)=\frac{-35-13\sqrt{13}}2$, $x(0)=0$ and $x(5)=-35$ metres.
$\begin{align*}\text{Distance}&=|x(r)|+|x(s)-x(r)|+|-35-x(s)|\\&=\frac{-35+13\sqrt{13}}2+13\sqrt{13}+\frac{-35+13\sqrt{13}}2\\&=26\sqrt{13}-35\text{ m}\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: A particle has displacement $x(t)=2te^{-t}$ metres for $t\ge0$ seconds. Show that it changes direction exactly once and find its displacement then.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Using the product rule:
$\begin{align*}v(t)&=2e^{-t}-2te^{-t}\\&=2(1-t)e^{-t}\end{align*}$
Since $e^{-t}>0$, velocity is zero only at $t=1$. It is positive for $0\le t<1$ and negative for $t>1$. The particle therefore changes direction exactly once, at $1$ s.
$\begin{align*}x(1)&=2e^{-1}\\&=\frac2e\text{ m}\end{align*}$

foundation.question_text:
A particle has acceleration $a = 6t - 4\text{ m/s}^{2}$ and initial velocity $v(0) = 5\text{ m/s}$.
Find $v$ as a function of $t$.

A particle has acceleration $a = 12t^{2} + 2\text{ m/s}^{2}$, and $v = 10\text{ m/s}$ when $t = 1$.
Find $v$ as a function of $t$.

A particle has velocity $v = 3t^{2} - 8t\text{ m/s}$ and initial displacement $x(0) = 2\text{ m}$.
Find $x$ as a function of $t$.

A particle has velocity $v = 4 - 2t\text{ m/s}$, and $x = 7\text{ m}$ when $t = 2$.
Find $x$ as a function of $t$.

A particle has acceleration $a = 12t\text{ m/s}^{2}$, with $v(0) = -3\text{ m/s}$ and $x(0) = 1\text{ m}$.
Find $x$ as a function of $t$.
foundation.solution_text:
$v = \displaystyle\int 12t\,dt$
$= 6t^{2} + c$
$\text{When } t = 0,\ v = -3:\ c = -3$
$v = 6t^{2} - 3$
$x = \displaystyle\int (6t^{2} - 3)\,dt$
$= 2t^{3} - 3t + d$
$\text{When } t = 0,\ x = 1:\ d = 1$
$x = 2t^{3} - 3t + 1$

foundation.question_text:
A particle has displacement $x = t^{3} + 2t$ metres at time $t$ seconds.
Find its displacement between $t = 1$ and $t = 3$.

A particle has velocity $v = 6t + 2\text{ m/s}$ for $t \ge 0$.
Find its displacement over the first $4$ seconds.

At time $t = 2$ a particle has velocity $v = -5\text{ m/s}$ and acceleration $a = -3\text{ m/s}^{2}$.
Is the particle speeding up or slowing down?
Give a reason.
foundation.solution_text:
$v = -5,\ a = -3$
$\text{Both are negative, so } v \text{ and } a \text{ have the same sign.}$
The particle is speeding up.

foundation.question_text:
At time $t = 3$ a particle has velocity $v = 8\text{ m/s}$ and acceleration $a = -2\text{ m/s}^{2}$.
Is the particle speeding up or slowing down?
Give a reason.
foundation.solution_text:
$v = 8,\ a = -2$
$\text{The signs are opposite, so the speed } |v| \text{ is decreasing.}$
The particle is slowing down.

development.question_text:
A particle has acceleration $a = 6t - 10\text{ m/s}^{2}$, with $v(0) = 4\text{ m/s}$ and $x(0) = -2\text{ m}$.
Find $v$ and $x$ as functions of $t$.

A particle moves with $x = t^{3} - 6t^{2} + 5$ metres for $t \ge 0$.
Find the time at which the particle changes direction, and justify that the direction does change there.
development.solution_text:
$v = \dot{x} = 3t^{2} - 12t$
$\text{Set } v = 0:$
$3t(t - 4) = 0$
$t = 0\text{ or } t = 4$
$\text{For } 0 < t < 4,\ v < 0\text{ (e.g. } v(1) = -9)$
$\text{For } t > 4,\ v > 0\text{ (e.g. } v(5) = 15)$
The velocity changes sign at $t = 4$, so the particle changes direction at $t = 4$ seconds.

development.question_text:
A particle moves with $x = t^{4} - 8t^{2}$ metres for $t \ge 0$.
Find the time at which the particle changes direction.
development.solution_text:
$v = \dot{x} = 4t^{3} - 16t$
$\text{Set } v = 0:$
$4t(t - 2)(t + 2) = 0$
$t = 0,\ t = 2\text{ or } t = -2$
$\text{Since } t \ge 0,\ \text{the interior solution is } t = 2$
$v(1) = -12\text{ and } v(3) = 60$
The velocity changes sign at $t = 2$, so the particle changes direction at $t = 2$ seconds.

development.question_text:
A particle moves with $x = t^{2} - 6t + 8$ metres for $0 \le t \le 5$ seconds.
Find (a) its displacement over this interval and (b) the distance it travels over this interval.

A particle has velocity $v = 3t^{2} - 12\text{ m/s}$ and starts at the origin, $x(0) = 0$.
Find the distance it travels in the first $3$ seconds.

A particle moves with $x = t^{3} - 2t^{2}$ metres for $3 \le t \le 5$ seconds.
Find its displacement over this interval.

A particle moves with $x = t^{3} - 6t^{2} + 4t$ metres for $t \ge 0$.
Is the particle speeding up or slowing down when $t = 3$?
Give a reason.
development.solution_text:
$v = \dot{x} = 3t^{2} - 12t + 4$
$a = \ddot{x} = 6t - 12$
$v(3) = 27 - 36 + 4$
$= -5\text{ m/s}$
$a(3) = 18 - 12$
$= 6\text{ m/s}^{2}$
$\text{The signs are opposite, so the speed } |v| \text{ is decreasing.}$
The particle is slowing down, even though the acceleration is positive.

development.question_text:
The velocity–time graph of a particle moving in a straight line is shown, where $v = t^{2} - 6t + 8\text{ m/s}$ for $0 \le t \le 6$ seconds.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[every node/.style={font=\large}]
\begin{axis}[axis lines=middle, xlabel={$t$ (s)}, ylabel={$v$ (m/s)},
             xmin=-0.6, xmax=6.8, ymin=-3, ymax=9.5,
             xtick={1,2,3,4,5,6}, ytick={-2,2,4,6,8}, samples=100, clip=false,
             width=10cm, height=8cm]
\addplot[thick, domain=0:6] {x*x - 6*x + 8};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]
State the times at which the particle is at rest, and the interval during which it moves in the negative direction.
development.solution_text:
$\text{At rest where } v = 0:$
$t^{2} - 6t + 8 = 0$
$(t - 2)(t - 4) = 0$
$t = 2\text{ s and } t = 4\text{ s}$
$\text{The graph is below the } t\text{-axis between these times.}$
The particle moves in the negative direction for $2 < t < 4$.

development.question_text:
The displacement–time graph of a particle moving in a straight line is shown, where $x = 4t - t^{2}$ metres for $0 \le t \le 5$ seconds.
[tikz]
\begin{tikzpicture}[every node/.style={font=\large}]
\begin{axis}[axis lines=middle, xlabel={$t$ (s)}, ylabel={$x$ (m)},
             xmin=-0.6, xmax=5.8, ymin=-6.5, ymax=5.5,
             xtick={1,2,3,4,5}, ytick={-6,-4,-2,2,4}, samples=100, clip=false,
             width=10cm, height=8cm]
\addplot[thick, domain=0:5] {4*x - x*x};
\end{axis}
\end{tikzpicture}
[/tikz]
Find the time at which the particle is at rest, and explain why this is not the same as the time it is at the origin.
development.solution_text:
$v = \dot{x} = 4 - 2t$
$\text{At rest, } v = 0:$
$4 - 2t = 0$
$t = 2\text{ s}$
$x(2) = 8 - 4$
$= 4\text{ m}$
$\text{At the origin, } x = 0:$
$t(4 - t) = 0$
$t = 0\text{ s and } t = 4\text{ s}$
At rest means the velocity is zero, which happens at the turning point $t = 2$ where the particle is $4$ m from the origin; the particle is at the origin at $t = 0$ and $t = 4$, where it is moving.

development.question_text:
A particle has acceleration $a = 6\cos 3t\text{ m/s}^{2}$ and initial velocity $v(0) = 2\text{ m/s}$.
Find $v$ as a function of $t$.

mastery.question_text:
A particle has acceleration $a = 6t - 24\text{ m/s}^{2}$, with $v(0) = 36\text{ m/s}$ and $x(0) = 0\text{ m}$.
Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first $7$ seconds.

A particle moves with $x = t^{3} - 9t^{2} + 15t + 2$ metres for $0 \le t \le 6$ seconds.
Find every interval on which the particle is speeding up.
mastery.solution_text:
$v = \dot{x} = 3t^{2} - 18t + 15$
$= 3(t - 1)(t - 5)$
$a = \ddot{x} = 6t - 18$
$v = 0\text{ at } t = 1,\ t = 5;\ a = 0\text{ at } t = 3$
$\text{On } 0 < t < 1:\ v > 0,\ a < 0$
$\text{On } 1 < t < 3:\ v < 0,\ a < 0$
$\text{On } 3 < t < 5:\ v < 0,\ a > 0$
$\text{On } 5 < t < 6:\ v > 0,\ a > 0$
The signs of $v$ and $a$ agree on $1 < t < 3$ and on $5 < t < 6$, so the particle is speeding up on those intervals.

mastery.question_text:
A particle has acceleration $a = 12t - 6\text{ m/s}^{2}$.
It is at $x = 4\text{ m}$ when $t = 0$ and at $x = 5\text{ m}$ when $t = 1$.
Find $x$ as a function of $t$.

A particle moves with $x = te^{-t}$ metres for $t \ge 0$.
Show that the particle changes direction exactly once, and find its displacement at that time.
mastery.solution_text:
$v = \dot{x} = e^{-t} - te^{-t}$
$= (1 - t)e^{-t}$
$\text{Since } e^{-t} > 0,\ v = 0\text{ only when } t = 1$
$\text{For } 0 \le t < 1,\ v > 0;\ \text{for } t > 1,\ v < 0$
$\text{The velocity changes sign once, at } t = 1\text{ s.}$
$x(1) = 1 \times e^{-1}$
$= e^{-1}\text{ m}$
